lead: A combustion chamber is the space the burning charge fills. Its shape sets mixing, flame speed, and whether hot metal or carbon ignites the charge on its own. In an SI engine the mixture is prepared outside the cylinder, so the chamber burns it quickly without knock. In a CI engine fuel is injected into hot air, so the chamber moves air and spreads the spray. Wedge, hemispherical and bathtub chambers are SI types; bowl-in-piston and prechamber chambers are CI types.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.1 on SI stages, 3.4 on knock, 3.5 on CI stages and 3.7 on swirl, squish and tumble.

blocks.text: The combustion chamber is the space above the piston at top dead centre. Its volume is the clearance volume V<sub>c</sub>. Its shape decides mixing, burn rate and knock. Every design is a compromise between these demands.

items: Good mixing. Turbulence and squish bring fuel and air together. In CI engines mixing time is only a few milliseconds.
Short flame travel. The flame should start near the centre and reach the far wall quickly; late-burning end gas knocks.
No hot spots. Sharp edges, a hot exhaust valve, a protruding plug tip or glowing carbon can ignite the charge before the spark.
Good breathing. Large valves and open ports raise volumetric efficiency and power.
Low heat loss. A compact chamber has less wall area, so less heat escapes and cold starting is easier.

blocks.where: CR is compression ratio (no unit); V<sub>s</sub> is swept volume in cm³; V<sub>c</sub> is clearance volume in cm³. Any piston bowl is part of V<sub>c</sub>.

sections.h3: SI chamber shapes: wedge, hemispherical, bathtub

blocks.text: An SI engine prepares its mixture outside the cylinder, so the chamber only has to burn it fast and without knock. Three shapes cover most engines.

items: Wedge chamber. The head is a shallow wedge with tilted valves in a row. The rising piston squeezes air from the thin end; that squish adds turbulence near the plug. It is cheap, gives good squish, and suits two-valve pushrod engines. Flame travel across the wedge is long, so large-bore versions knock more easily.

Hemispherical chamber. The head is a dome, valves are inclined on both sides and the plug is central. Flame travel is shortest, breathing is best because large valves fit, and high compression ratios suit it. The dome encloses its volume with the smallest wall area of the three shapes, so heat loss is low. Its drawback is negligible squish, that is, low turbulence, which slows the burn at part load; higher unburnt hydrocarbon comes from wall quenching and poor turbulence, not from a large surface area.

Bathtub chamber. A flat head with a shallow tub-shaped recess over the piston and valves in line. It is simple and cheap, gives useful squish and swirl, and is common on small two-valve engines. Breathing is weaker than a hemispherical head because the valves cannot be made large.

blocks.text: Squish and swirl (Chapter 3.7) separate these shapes in practice. The wedge and bathtub generate squish; the hemispherical does not.

sections.h3: CI chambers: direct and indirect injection

blocks.text: A diesel engine injects fuel into hot air, so its chamber must move air and spread the spray. Two families exist.

items: Direct injection (DI). The chamber is open and fuel is sprayed into a bowl in the piston crown. A helical inlet port makes swirl, and the rising piston pushes squish flow into the bowl. The bowl may be shallow and wide (toroidal) or deep with a re-entrant lip that turns the spray upward. Injection pressure is high, the spray must match the bowl and swirl, and fuel economy and cold starting are best. It is noisier because the premixed burn is sharp.

Indirect injection (IDI). The chamber is divided. Fuel is sprayed into a small prechamber or swirl chamber joined to the main chamber by a narrow throat. During compression air rushes in through the throat; combustion starts there and the burning jet shoots back, mixing hard. Injection pressure can be low, the burn is smoother and quieter, and the engine runs over a wider speed range. The throat surface loses heat, so fuel economy is poorer and a glow plug is often needed for cold starting.

blocks.text: The delay period and diesel knock (3.5, 3.6) depend on which layout you have.

items: Bore. Flame travel grows roughly with half the bore. A large bore in an SI engine lengthens the flame path and increases knock, so big petrol engines use a central plug or two plugs.

Compression ratio. A high CR raises thermal efficiency but also peak pressure and temperature. In SI engines it is limited by knock; in CI engines a high CR shortens ignition delay and helps cold starting.
Valve size and number. Four valves allow a central plug or injector, better breathing and a compact chamber. Two valves restrict valve area and push the plug to one side.

Injection location and spray. In DI the injector is central and the spray angle must fit the bowl; a wrong angle wets the wall and makes smoke. In IDI the injector sits in the prechamber, aimed at the throat.
Cooling. The exhaust valve side runs hottest and glows first, so the chamber keeps the plug and end gas away from it. Cooling system design is in Unit 4.

figure.caption: The two families of chamber. Notice that spark ignition has three common shapes, while compression ignition splits into an open bowl in the piston and a divided prechamber.

spec.aria: Tree of combustion chambers: SI types are wedge, hemispherical and bathtub; CI types are direct injection with a piston bowl and indirect injection with a prechamber.

examples.question: A CI engine has bore 100 mm and stroke 110 mm. Its DI bowl is 55 mm diameter and 18 mm deep. Clearance volume is 70 cm³. Estimate the bowl volume as a cylinder and its percentage of clearance volume.
steps: Convert: d = 5.5 cm, h = 1.8 cm, V<sub>c</sub> = 70 cm³.
The bowl holds most of the clearance volume in a DI engine; here it is about 61 %, the rest being the squish gap above the crown.
examples.answer: The bowl volume is about 42.76 cm³, which is about 61.1 % of the 70 cm³ clearance volume.
examples.check:
import math
d = 5.5   # bowl diameter, cm
h = 1.8   # bowl depth, cm
Vc = 70.0  # clearance volume, cm3
Vb = math.pi / 4 * d ** 2 * h
print(round(Vb, 2))
print(round(Vb / Vc * 100, 1))

examples.question: A shallow toroidal bowl in a DI diesel is 60 mm diameter and 12 mm deep. Clearance volume is 55 cm³. Find bowl volume and fraction of clearance volume.
steps: The two bowls give nearly the same fraction only because the clearances differ; in general the volume goes as d² × h, so a given percentage change in diameter changes the volume twice as much as the same percentage change in depth.
examples.answer: The bowl volume is about 33.93 cm³, about 61.7 % of the clearance volume.
examples.check:
import math
d = 6.0
h = 1.2
Vc = 55.0
Vb = math.pi / 4 * d ** 2 * h
print(round(Vb, 2))
print(round(Vb / Vc * 100, 1))

traps: A prechamber engine is indirect injection (IDI). 'Direct injection with a prechamber' is wrong; in DI fuel goes into a piston bowl.
The bowl is inside V<sub>c</sub>. Do not add it again when calculating compression ratio.
Wedge, bathtub and hemispherical are SI shapes; bowl-in-piston and prechamber are CI. A mixed list question is common.
Convert bowl depth from mm to cm before comparing with V<sub>c</sub> in cm³.
The hemispherical chamber has good breathing but low squish. Do not claim high turbulence; it relies on short flame travel instead.

quiz.q: Name the three common SI combustion chamber shapes.
What is indirect injection (IDI) in a diesel engine?
quiz.a: A divided chamber layout in which fuel is injected into a prechamber or swirl chamber connected to the main chamber by a narrow throat.

quiz.q: Why does a hemispherical chamber breathe better but need more spark advance at part load?
quiz.a: Large inclined valves give high volumetric efficiency. Almost no squish means poor stirring, so the flame burns slowly and the spark must be advanced at part load.

quiz.q: Why does an IDI diesel give lower fuel efficiency than a DI diesel?
quiz.a: The throat and extra prechamber surface add heat and throttling losses. DI has a compact open chamber with less wall area, so efficiency is higher.

quiz.q: A DI diesel has a bowl 60 mm diameter and 15 mm deep, with clearance volume 65 cm³. Estimate the bowl volume as a cylinder and its percentage of clearance volume.
Why does a large bore make an SI engine more knock-prone, and what do designers do about it?
quiz.a: Flame travel grows with bore, so end gas is heated longer before the flame arrives and may autoignite. Designers centralise the plug, use a compact chamber, add squish, and use two plugs in very large bores.

quiz.q: Why must the injector position and spray angle match the bowl shape in a DI diesel?
quiz.a: The spray must meet swirling air inside the bowl, not the wall. A wall film burns late and makes smoke; a spray that misses the bowl mixes too slowly and lengthens ignition delay.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern car diesels use a re-entrant bowl with a central multi-hole injector and high injection pressure; the bowl is tuned in CFD before machining. Petrol engines use a pent-roof head with a central plug under four valves, a refined hemispherical idea. Optical engines and laser diagnostics study mixing (Unit 6). Low-temperature modes such as HCCI and RCCI need mixing before ignition rather than after injection. Search terms: pent-roof chamber, re-entrant bowl, squish area ratio, spray-bowl matching.
